# Plan: Stall Sense, Day 1 setup (Tue Oct 13)

## Context
devhack.md (the project brief) sets out the Hacktoberfest Week 2 entry: a local tool for farmers market vendors. Gemma (vision, via Ollama) reads handwritten tally photos, and TabPFN forecasts how much of each item to bring. The folder holds only devhack.md for now. This plan covers the Day 1 "first actions" (section 10, items 4 to 7) so that Wednesday can start on extraction and forecasting.

Facts so far:
- Hardware: Apple M4, 10 CPU cores, 16 GB unified memory, 65 GB free disk, macOS 15.5. This runs a ~4B Gemma vision model well. Avoid models above ~12B. TabPFN on CPU is fine for a few hundred rows.
- Installed: git and system Python 3.9.6 only. No Homebrew, uv, Ollama or gh.
- Parth: reads Python but rarely writes it. Has 2 to 3 h/day. No vendor lined up yet. Name chosen: **Stall Sense** (stallsense.tech).

Scope decision: at 2 to 3 h/day, the stretch goals (Tinker, Render, Sentry) are cut now rather than on Thursday. The time goes to the MVP, the backtest and the post. "My First User" stays optional, and the section gets deleted if no vendor turns up by Friday.

## Steps

1. **Update devhack.md**: rename to Stall Sense, mark "Hardware checked" and "Name picked", and add Decision Log entries (name, Gemma size, stretch goals cut, no vendor yet). Copy it to `CLAUDE.md` so future sessions load it on their own. devhack.md stays as is.

2. **Repo skeleton** (section 3 layout): `app/`, `extract/`, `forecast/`, `data/{synthetic,real,samples}/`, `docs/`, plus:
   - `.gitignore`: `.env`, `.venv/`, model caches, `data/real/`, `__pycache__/`, `.DS_Store`
   - `.env.example` (TABPFN token placeholder, `TABPFN_MODEL_CACHE_DIR`)
   - `EVIDENCE.md` (headings: Timings, Failures & fixes, Screenshots, Cost comparison, Feedback)
   - `POST_DRAFT.md` (the section 9 template, verbatim)
   - `README.md` (short stub)
   - `git init` locally. Parth creates the public GitHub repo on github.com himself, since gh isn't installed and the repo is public. I then add the remote.

3. **Python environment without sudo**: install `uv` with its official user-level installer. Then `uv python install 3.12` and `uv venv`, and add `requirements.txt` with `tabpfn`, `streamlit`, `pandas`, `ollama`, `pillow`, `requests`. Before pinning, I check the current TabPFN docs and PyPI for the right package and version for TabPFN-3.5 and how its license and token flow works (the brief says not to rely on memory).

4. **Agent session capture** (section 7): read the DevRelay and Entire docs on capturing Claude Code sessions, give Parth the steps in plain language, and set up whatever can be set up locally. This happens before heavy building so early sessions aren't lost. Needs Parth for any account signups.

5. **Ollama + Gemma smoke test**: Parth installs the Ollama macOS app from ollama.com (a GUI install, so I can't do it from here). I check the Ollama library for current Gemma vision variants, then pull the smallest vision model that can plausibly read handwriting (~4B class). I time one test image, write the time to EVIDENCE.md, and step up a size only if the readings are poor.

6. **TabPFN smoke test**: Parth signs up at platform.priorlabs.ai and accepts the non-commercial license. I run a tiny fit/predict on toy data with the version set in a single config switch (`forecast/config.py`), log the fit and predict times, then repeat with Wi-Fi off to confirm the cache works offline.

7. **Start the synthetic data generator** (`data/synthetic/generate.py`): one vendor, about 6 to 8 items, 2 seasons of weekly Saturday markets. Weather comes from Open-Meteo historical data for a real city (Delhi/Noida, matching the local framing). Includes crop seasonality, a rain/heat/holiday attendance effect, noise, and `sold = min(demand, brought)` so sellouts are censored. Output is a CSV labeled SIMULATED in the filename and in a column. Commented clearly so Parth can read it.

Things Parth has to do himself (I'll prompt at each step): install Ollama, sign up at Prior Labs, claim the .tech domain at hacktoberfest.com/my/promos (and turn off auto renew later), create the GitHub repo, and sign up for DevRelay/Entire.

## Verification
- `uv run python -c "import tabpfn, streamlit, ollama"` succeeds.
- `ollama run <gemma-vision> "describe" < test image` returns text, and the time is logged in EVIDENCE.md.
- The TabPFN toy predict works with the network off.
- `uv run python data/synthetic/generate.py` writes a CSV. Spot checks: no sold > brought, out-of-season items at zero, and rainy weeks lower on average.
- `git status` shows no `.env`, weights or caches tracked.

- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message

- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve

entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

Entire CLI is an open-source tool that hooks into Git to record AI coding agent sessions alongside commits. It works with Claude Code, and the search results describe the following:

content.content:
**macOS install options**
- **Homebrew (stable):** `brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire`. Use the fully-qualified name. The page says it "requires Homebrew 6.0.10 or newer."
- **Homebrew (nightly):** `brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire@nightly`
- **Install script (stable):** `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash`
- **Install script (nightly):** `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly`
- **Go:** `go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire@latest`. Also install `git-remote-entire` if you need `entire://` URLs. Go 1.27.1+ is required.
- **Direct binary download:** not described on the page.

**Commands**
- `entire enable` sets up the current repo. Use `entire enable --agent claude-code` to skip the prompts.
- `entire agent add claude-code` adds an agent, and `entire agent remove claude-code` removes one.

**Sharing sessions publicly**
The page doesn't describe a feature for publishing sessions or any entire.io web links for sharing. It only says that "If your repository is public, this data is visible to anyone," because transcripts live in the repo's checkpoint refs.

**Account and login**
The page lists `entire login` and `entire logout` as account commands, and says `entire login` opens a browser by default. It doesn't say whether login is required for basic local use. Its requirements list only Git, a supported OS, and an installed, authenticated agent.

**Pricing**
Not mentioned.

**What gets pushed to the remote**
- Checkpoint data rides along with your normal pushes, but only to one elected remote. Entire picks `checkpoint_push_remote` if set, then the remote your branch pushes to, then `origin`, then the sole remote, then the first remote in config order.
- Pushes to other remotes carry no checkpoint data, unless they point to the same GitHub repository.
- Each checkpoint is stored under `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`. It contains `metadata.json`, transcript files, and subagent task records.
- Auto-push is controlled by `strategy_options.push_sessions`, which defaults to `true`.
- Entire never creates commits on your active branch.
- Secret redaction is "best-effort," according to the page.

"""
Synthetic sales history for ONE market vendor. ALL OUTPUT IS SIMULATED.

Why this exists: there is no public dataset of per-vendor, per-item market
sales. So we simulate a realistic one, grounded in real things:
  * real historical weather for a real city (Open-Meteo, free, no key)
  * crop seasons (items appear and disappear through the year)
  * fewer shoppers on rainy, very hot or very cold days, more before holidays
  * the key detail: you can't sell more than you brought. If demand is higher,
    the vendor SELLS OUT and the true demand is hidden. Forecasters must cope.

Run:  uv run python data/synthetic/generate.py
Out:  data/synthetic/SIMULATED_sales_<city>.csv
"""

import json
from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import requests

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# SETTINGS: change the city here. Everything else adapts.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
CITY = {
    "name": "portland_or",
    "lat": 45.52,
    "lon": -122.68,
    "timezone": "America/Los_Angeles",
    # Dates that bring extra shoppers the market before (edit per city).
    "holidays": ["2024-11-28", "2024-12-25", "2025-05-26", "2025-07-04",
                 "2025-09-01", "2025-11-27", "2025-12-25", "2026-05-25",
                 "2026-07-04", "2026-09-07"],
}
START = date(2024, 10, 5)   # first market day (a Saturday)
END = date(2026, 10, 3)     # last market day with weather data available
SEED = 42                   # same seed -> same data every run

# Two weekly markets the vendor attends: (name, weekday 0=Mon, crowd size)
MARKETS = [("saturday_market", 5, 1.0), ("wednesday_market", 2, 0.55)]

# Items: unit, base weekly demand at the Saturday market, price, cost to
# grow/make (per unit), and months in season (northern hemisphere).
ALL_YEAR = list(range(1, 13))
ITEMS = {
    "kale":         ("bunch",  30, 4.0, 1.2, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12]),
    "tomatoes":     ("kg",     25, 7.0, 2.5, [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]),
    "strawberries": ("punnet", 40, 6.0, 2.0, [5, 6, 7]),
    "zucchini":     ("kg",     18, 5.0, 1.5, [6, 7, 8, 9]),
    "apples":       ("kg",     22, 5.5, 1.8, [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 1]),
    "eggs":         ("dozen",  20, 8.0, 3.5, ALL_YEAR),
    "sourdough":    ("loaf",   24, 9.0, 2.5, ALL_YEAR),
    "honey":        ("jar",     8, 12.0, 4.0, ALL_YEAR),
}

OUT_DIR = Path(__file__).parent


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 1: real daily weather (cached to disk so later runs work offline)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def load_weather() -> pd.DataFrame:
    cache = OUT_DIR / f"weather_{CITY['name']}.json"
    if not cache.exists():
        resp = requests.get(
            "https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive",
            params={
                "latitude": CITY["lat"], "longitude": CITY["lon"],
                "start_date": START.isoformat(), "end_date": END.isoformat(),
                "daily": "temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum",
                "timezone": CITY["timezone"],
            },
            timeout=30,
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
        cache.write_text(resp.text)
    daily = json.loads(cache.read_text())["daily"]
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "date": pd.to_datetime(daily["time"]).date,
        "temp_max_c": daily["temperature_2m_max"],
        "rain_mm": daily["precipitation_sum"],
    }).set_index("date")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 2: helpers for seasons and crowd size
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def in_season(months: list[int], d: date) -> bool:
    month = d.month
    if CITY["lat"] < 0:                     # southern hemisphere: flip seasons
        month = (month + 5) % 12 + 1
    return month in months


def crowd_factor(temp: float, rain: float, d: date) -> float:
    """How busy the market is compared with a normal day (1.0)."""
    f = 1.0
    f *= 1 - min(0.45, rain * 0.03)         # rain keeps people home
    if temp >= 32:
        f *= 0.85                           # too hot
    if temp <= 3:
        f *= 0.85                           # too cold
    holidays = [date.fromisoformat(h) for h in CITY["holidays"]]
    if any(0 < (h - d).days <= 7 for h in holidays):
        f *= 1.25                           # shopping before a holiday
    return f


def is_holiday_week(d: date) -> bool:
    return any(0 < (date.fromisoformat(h) - d).days <= 7 for h in CITY["holidays"])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 3: simulate every market day
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def simulate() -> pd.DataFrame:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    weather = load_weather()
    last_sold, last_brought, sold_out_last = {}, {}, {}
    rows = []

    d = START
    while d <= END:
        for market, weekday, crowd in MARKETS:
            if d.weekday() != weekday or d not in weather.index:
                continue
            temp = float(weather.loc[d, "temp_max_c"])
            rain = float(weather.loc[d, "rain_mm"])
            busy = crowd_factor(temp, rain, d)
            growth = 1 + 0.08 * (d - START).days / 365   # slowly growing business

            for item, (unit, base, price, cost, months) in ITEMS.items():
                if not in_season(months, d):
                    continue                # vendor doesn't bring it, no row
                key = (market, item)

                # True demand (what shoppers WANT). Never seen directly.
                mean = base * crowd * busy * growth
                demand = rng.poisson(mean * rng.lognormal(0, 0.12))

                # Vendor's guess, the pen-and-paper way: last time's sales,
                # a bit more if they sold out, plus gut-feel noise.
                if key in last_sold:
                    guess = last_sold[key] * (1.25 if sold_out_last[key] else 1.05)
                else:
                    guess = base * crowd    # first time: rough guess
                brought = max(1, int(round(guess * rng.normal(1.0, 0.1))))

                sold = min(demand, brought) # can't sell what you didn't bring
                sold_out = demand >= brought

                rows.append({
                    "date": d.isoformat(), "weekday": d.strftime("%a"),
                    "market": market, "item": item, "unit": unit,
                    "brought": brought, "sold": sold, "leftover": brought - sold,
                    "sold_out": sold_out, "price": price, "unit_cost": cost,
                    "temp_max_c": temp, "rain_mm": rain,
                    "holiday_week": is_holiday_week(d),
                    "true_demand": demand,  # for evaluation only, never a feature
                    "data_source": "SIMULATED",
                })
                last_sold[key], last_brought[key], sold_out_last[key] = sold, brought, sold_out
        d += timedelta(days=1)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    df = simulate()
    out = OUT_DIR / f"SIMULATED_sales_{CITY['name']}.csv"
    df.to_csv(out, index=False)
    print(f"Wrote {len(df)} rows to {out}")
    print(f"Market days: {df['date'].nunique()}, items: {df['item'].nunique()}")
    print(f"Sellout rate: {df['sold_out'].mean():.0%}, "
          f"leftover units: {df['leftover'].sum()}")

    "holidays": ["2024-11-28", "2024-12-25", "2025-05-26", "2025-07-04",
                 "2025-09-01", "2025-11-27", "2025-12-25", "2026-05-25",
                 "2026-07-04", "2026-09-07"],
}
START = date(2024, 10, 5)   # first market day (a Saturday)
END = date(2026, 10, 3)     # last market day with weather data available
SEED = 42                   # same seed -> same data every run

# Two weekly markets the vendor attends: (name, weekday 0=Mon, crowd size)
MARKETS = [("saturday_market", 5, 1.0), ("wednesday_market", 2, 0.55)]

# Items: unit, base weekly demand at the Saturday market, price, cost to
# grow/make (per unit), and months in season (northern hemisphere).
ALL_YEAR = list(range(1, 13))
ITEMS = {
    "kale":         ("bunch",  30, 4.0, 1.2, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12]),
    "tomatoes":     ("kg",     25, 7.0, 2.5, [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]),
    "strawberries": ("punnet", 40, 6.0, 2.0, [5, 6, 7]),
    "zucchini":     ("kg",     18, 5.0, 1.5, [6, 7, 8, 9]),
    "apples":       ("kg",     22, 5.5, 1.8, [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 1]),
    "eggs":         ("dozen",  20, 8.0, 3.5, ALL_YEAR),
    "sourdough":    ("loaf",   24, 9.0, 2.5, ALL_YEAR),
    "honey":        ("jar",     8, 12.0, 4.0, ALL_YEAR),
}

OUT_DIR = Path(__file__).parent


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 1: real daily weather (cached to disk so later runs work offline)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def load_weather() -> pd.DataFrame:
    cache = OUT_DIR / f"weather_{CITY['name']}.json"
    if not cache.exists():
        resp = requests.get(
            "https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive",
            params={
                "latitude": CITY["lat"], "longitude": CITY["lon"],
                "start_date": START.isoformat(), "end_date": END.isoformat(),
                "daily": "temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum",
                "timezone": CITY["timezone"],
            },
            timeout=30,
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
        cache.write_text(resp.text)
    daily = json.loads(cache.read_text())["daily"]
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "date": pd.to_datetime(daily["time"]).date,
        "temp_max_c": daily["temperature_2m_max"],
        "rain_mm": daily["precipitation_sum"],
    }).set_index("date")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 2: helpers for seasons and crowd size
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def in_season(months: list[int], d: date) -> bool:
    month = d.month
    if CITY["lat"] < 0:                     # southern hemisphere: flip seasons
        month = (month + 5) % 12 + 1
    return month in months


def crowd_factor(temp: float, rain: float, d: date) -> float:
    """How busy the market is compared with a normal day (1.0)."""
    f = 1.0
    f *= 1 - min(0.45, rain * 0.03)         # rain keeps people home
    if temp >= 32:
        f *= 0.85                           # too hot
    if temp <= 3:
        f *= 0.85                           # too cold
    holidays = [date.fromisoformat(h) for h in CITY["holidays"]]
    if any(0 < (h - d).days <= 7 for h in holidays):
        f *= 1.25                           # shopping before a holiday
    return f


def is_holiday_week(d: date) -> bool:
    return any(0 < (date.fromisoformat(h) - d).days <= 7 for h in CITY["holidays"])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 3: simulate every market day
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def simulate() -> pd.DataFrame:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    weather = load_weather()
    last_sold, last_brought, sold_out_last = {}, {}, {}
    rows = []

    d = START
    while d <= END:
        for market, weekday, crowd in MARKETS:
            if d.weekday() != weekday or d not in weather.index:
                continue
            temp = float(weather.loc[d, "temp_max_c"])
            rain = float(weather.loc[d, "rain_mm"])
            busy = crowd_factor(temp, rain, d)
            growth = 1 + 0.08 * (d - START).days / 365   # slowly growing business

            for item, (unit, base, price, cost, months) in ITEMS.items():
                if not in_season(months, d):
                    continue                # vendor doesn't bring it, no row
                key = (market, item)

                # True demand (what shoppers WANT). Never seen directly.
                mean = base * crowd * busy * growth
                demand = rng.poisson(mean * rng.lognormal(0, 0.12))

                # Vendor's guess, the pen-and-paper way: sold out last time?
                # bring more than last time. Otherwise last sales plus a
                # small buffer. Then gut-feel noise.
                if key in last_sold:
                    if sold_out_last[key]:
                        guess = last_brought[key] * 1.2
                    else:
                        guess = last_sold[key] * 1.15
                else:
                    guess = base * crowd    # first time: rough guess
                brought = max(1, int(round(guess * rng.normal(1.0, 0.1))))

                sold = min(demand, brought) # can't sell what you didn't bring
                sold_out = demand >= brought

                rows.append({
                    "date": d.isoformat(), "weekday": d.strftime("%a"),
                    "market": market, "item": item, "unit": unit,
                    "brought": brought, "sold": sold, "leftover": brought - sold,
                    "sold_out": sold_out, "price": price, "unit_cost": cost,
                    "temp_max_c": temp, "rain_mm": rain,
                    "holiday_week": is_holiday_week(d),
                    "true_demand": demand,  # for evaluation only, never a feature
                    "data_source": "SIMULATED",
                })
                last_sold[key], last_brought[key], sold_out_last[key] = sold, brought, sold_out
        d += timedelta(days=1)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    df = simulate()
    out = OUT_DIR / f"SIMULATED_sales_{CITY['name']}.csv"
    df.to_csv(out, index=False)
    print(f"Wrote {len(df)} rows to {out}")
    print(f"Market days: {df['date'].nunique()}, items: {df['item'].nunique()}")
    print(f"Sellout rate: {df['sold_out'].mean():.0%}, "
          f"leftover units: {df['leftover'].sum()}")

+                # a safety buffer, but don't cut back too sharply. Then

The framing is global now. I took the city reference out of [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) and saved this as a lasting preference so later sessions follow it too. [devhack.md](devhack.md) still has the original line; I left it alone because it's your file.

**Synthetic data:** [generate.py](data/synthetic/generate.py) is written and has run.
- **City:** the setting at the top of the file defaults to Portland, Oregon, with real weather from Open-Meteo. Seasons flip automatically for a southern-hemisphere city.
- **Size:** 2 years of data, 209 market days, 8 items (kale, tomatoes, strawberries and so on), 1,098 rows, labelled SIMULATED in the filename and in a column.
- **Checks:** sales never exceed what was brought, items disappear out of season, and rainy days sell about 35% less.
- **One fix:** the simulated vendor first sold out 70% of the time because of a flaw in how I modelled their guessing. After the fix it's about 30%, with about $14k wasted and $9k in missed sales over 2 years. That's the "pen and paper" baseline TabPFN has to beat. I logged the bug in [EVIDENCE.md](EVIDENCE.md) because it shows why "bring what you sold last week" goes wrong.

**Gemma:** Ollama is running, and `gemma4:e4b` (the newest Gemma with vision, about 4B size) is still downloading in the background.

**Claiming the .tech domain:** the promos page needs a login, so I couldn't see its exact steps. The usual flow is:
1. Go to [hacktoberfest.com](https://hacktoberfest.com) and sign in, or register (signing in with GitHub is easiest).
2. Open [hacktoberfest.com/my/promos](https://hacktoberfest.com/my/promos) and find the **.tech Domains** card. Copy the promo code, or follow the redeem link.
3. On [get.tech](https://get.tech), search for `stallsense.tech`, add it to the cart and apply the code. The total should come to $0.

5. After it's registered, turn off auto renew (it renews at $29.99 a year).

If there's no .tech card on the promos page, tell me what you see there and we'll work it out.

**Schedule:** it's Thursday and we're about two days behind. Still left: Gemma reading the tallies, the TabPFN forecast and backtest, and the Streamlit app. If you agree, I'll do Gemma and TabPFN tomorrow and the app on Saturday. That leaves Sunday for the post and video, with the hard deadline Monday at 12:29 PM IST.

input.content:
"""
Make realistic photos of handwritten tally sheets. ALL IMAGES ARE SIMULATED.

Why: no freely licensed photos of a market vendor's sales notebook exist
online, and to MEASURE how well Gemma reads a sheet we need to know the
correct answer. So we render sheets from the simulated sales history in
handwriting fonts, then make them messy like a real phone photo:
abbreviations, crossed-out numbers, "SOLD OUT" notes, a tilted page,
shadows, blur and JPEG compression.

Run:  uv run python data/samples/make_tallies.py
Out:  data/samples/tally_01.jpg ... and data/samples/labels.json (the answers)
"""

import json
import random
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFilter, ImageFont

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
SALES_CSV = HERE.parent / "synthetic" / "SIMULATED_sales_portland_or.csv"
FONTS = sorted((HERE / "fonts").glob("*.ttf"))
N_SHEETS = 12
SEED = 7

# How a busy vendor might scribble each item name.
ABBREVIATIONS = {
    "kale": ["kale", "Kale", "kale bunch"],
    "tomatoes": ["toms", "tomatos", "Tomatoes"],
    "strawberries": ["strawb", "strawbs", "Strwberries"],
    "zucchini": ["zukes", "zucc", "Zucchini"],
    "apples": ["apples", "Apls", "apples kg"],
    "eggs": ["eggs", "eggs (doz)", "Eggs"],
    "sourdough": ["sourdo", "loaves", "Sourdough"],
    "honey": ["honey", "hny jars", "Honey"],
}
MARKET_NAMES = {"saturday_market": ["Sat mkt", "SAT", "Saturday market"],
                "wednesday_market": ["Wed mkt", "WED", "Wednesday"]}


def handwritten(draw_on: Image.Image, xy, text, font, ink, rng):
    """Paste text with a slight random tilt and size wobble, like a pen."""
    size = int(font.size * rng.uniform(0.92, 1.08))
    f = font.font_variant(size=size)
    box = f.getbbox(text)
    w, h = box[2] + 20, box[3] + 20
    layer = Image.new("RGBA", (w, h), (0, 0, 0, 0))
    ImageDraw.Draw(layer).text((10, 10), text, font=f, fill=ink)
    layer = layer.rotate(rng.uniform(-3, 3), expand=True, resample=Image.BICUBIC)
    x, y = xy
    draw_on.alpha_composite(layer, (int(x + rng.uniform(-4, 4)), int(y + rng.uniform(-4, 4))))
    return f.getlength(text)


def strike(draw_on: Image.Image, x, y, width, font, ink):
    """A pen line through a mistaken number."""
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(draw_on)
    mid = y + font.size * 0.75
    d.line([(x - 3, mid + 4), (x + width + 6, mid - 4)], fill=ink, width=4)


def render_sheet(day: pd.DataFrame, rng: random.Random, messy: bool):
    """Draw one market day's tally on lined paper. Returns image + answer rows."""
    W, H = 1200, 1600
    paper = Image.new("RGBA", (W, H), (248, 245, 232, 255))
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(paper)
    for y in range(180, H, 70):                       # ruled lines
        d.line([(0, y), (W, y)], fill=(170, 195, 230, 255), width=2)
    d.line([(110, 0), (110, H)], fill=(225, 140, 140, 255), width=3)   # margin

    font = ImageFont.truetype(str(rng.choice(FONTS)), 58)
    ink = rng.choice([(25, 35, 90, 255), (20, 20, 20, 255), (40, 40, 120, 255)])

    first = day.iloc[0]
    date_fmt = rng.choice(["%d/%m/%y", "%a %d %b", "%m-%d"])
    header = f"{pd.Timestamp(first['date']).strftime(date_fmt)}   {rng.choice(MARKET_NAMES[first['market']])}"
    if first["rain_mm"] > 5 and rng.random() < 0.6:
        header += "  (rain!)"
    handwritten(paper, (140, 95), header, font, ink, rng)

    cols = {"item": 140, "took": 560, "sold": 760, "price": 980}
    labels = [("item", "item"), ("took", rng.choice(["took", "brought", "in"])),
              ("sold", "sold"), ("price", rng.choice(["$", "price", "@"]))]
    for key, text in labels:
        handwritten(paper, (cols[key], 190), text, font, ink, rng)

    answers = []
    rows = day.sample(frac=1, random_state=rng.randint(0, 9999)) if messy else day
    for i, (_, r) in enumerate(rows.iterrows()):
        y = 265 + i * 70
        handwritten(paper, (cols["item"], y), rng.choice(ABBREVIATIONS[r["item"]]), font, ink, rng)

        took = str(int(r["brought"]))
        if messy and rng.random() < 0.3:              # wrong number, crossed out
            wrong = str(int(r["brought"]) + rng.choice([-3, -2, 2, 5]))
            wlen = handwritten(paper, (cols["took"], y), wrong, font, ink, rng)
            strike(paper, cols["took"], y, wlen, font, ink)
            handwritten(paper, (cols["took"] + wlen + 18, y), took, font, ink, rng)
        else:
            handwritten(paper, (cols["took"], y), took, font, ink, rng)

        if r["sold_out"] and messy and rng.random() < 0.5:
            handwritten(paper, (cols["sold"], y), rng.choice(["all", "SOLD OUT", "all!"]), font, ink, rng)
        else:
            handwritten(paper, (cols["sold"], y), str(int(r["sold"])), font, ink, rng)

"""
Read a photo of a handwritten tally sheet into table rows, using Gemma
running locally through Ollama. Nothing leaves the laptop.

Use from Python:
    from extract.read_tally import read_tally
    result = read_tally("data/samples/tally_01.jpg")

Or from the terminal:
    uv run python -m extract.read_tally data/samples/tally_01.jpg
"""

import json
import sys
import time
from typing import Optional

import ollama
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

MODEL = "gemma4:e4b"     # change here to try a bigger/smaller Gemma

# The vendor's known items. In the app this comes from their sales history,
# so Gemma can map scribbles like "toms" or "sourdo" to a real item name.
KNOWN_ITEMS = ["kale", "tomatoes", "strawberries", "zucchini", "apples",
               "eggs", "sourdough", "honey"]


# The exact shape we want back. Ollama forces Gemma's answer to match it.
class Row(BaseModel):
    written_as: str = Field(description="item name exactly as written on the sheet")
    item: str = Field(description="matching name from the known item list, or 'unknown'")
    brought: Optional[int] = Field(description="quantity taken to market")
    sold: Optional[int] = Field(description="quantity sold")
    price: Optional[float] = Field(description="price per unit")
    unsure: bool = Field(description="true if any value in this row was hard to read")


class Tally(BaseModel):
    date_as_written: str
    market_as_written: str
    rows: list[Row]


PROMPT = f"""This is a photo of a market vendor's handwritten sales tally.
Read every item row into the schema.

Rules:
- Columns are: item, quantity brought (may be headed "took", "in" or "brought"),
  quantity sold, and price per unit (may be headed "$", "@" or "price").
- If a number is crossed out, ignore it and use the number written next to it.
- If "sold" says "all", "SOLD OUT" or similar, sold equals brought.
- Map each item to one of these known items: {", ".join(KNOWN_ITEMS)}.
  Abbreviations are common (e.g. "toms" = tomatoes). Use "unknown" if none fit.
- Set unsure=true for any row you could not read confidently. Never guess silently.
"""


def read_tally(image_path: str, model: str = MODEL) -> dict:
    """Send one photo to local Gemma and return its reading plus timing."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = ollama.chat(
        model=model,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT, "images": [image_path]}],
        format=Tally.model_json_schema(),
        options={"temperature": 0},
    )
    seconds = time.perf_counter() - start
    tally = Tally.model_validate_json(response.message.content)

    # "all" / "SOLD OUT" safety net, in case the model left sold empty.
    for row in tally.rows:
        if row.sold is None and row.brought is not None and not row.unsure:
            row.unsure = True
    return {"tally": tally.model_dump(), "seconds": round(seconds, 1), "model": model}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(read_tally(sys.argv[1]), indent=2))

"""
Score Gemma's readings against the known answers in data/samples/labels.json.
Produces the extraction accuracy numbers for EVIDENCE.md and the post.

Run:  uv run python -m extract.score            (all sample photos)
      uv run python -m extract.score tally_01.jpg tally_05.jpg
"""

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from extract.read_tally import MODEL, read_tally

SAMPLES = Path(__file__).parent.parent / "data" / "samples"
FIELDS = ["item", "brought", "sold", "price"]


def score_sheet(truth_rows: list[dict], read_rows: list[dict]) -> dict:
    """Field-level accuracy: for each true row, did Gemma get each field right?"""
    by_item = {r["item"]: r for r in read_rows}
    correct, total, unsure_flags, missed = 0, 0, 0, []
    for truth in truth_rows:
        got = by_item.get(truth["item"])
        for field in FIELDS:
            total += 1
            if got is None:
                continue
            if field == "price":
                ok = got["price"] is not None and abs(got["price"] - truth["price"]) < 0.01
            else:
                ok = got[field] == truth[field]
            correct += ok
            if not ok:
                missed.append(f"{truth['item']}.{field}: want {truth[field]}, got {got[field]}")
        if got is None:
            missed.append(f"{truth['item']}: row missing")
        elif got["unsure"]:
            unsure_flags += 1
    extra = len([r for r in read_rows if r["item"] not in {t["item"] for t in truth_rows}])
    return {"correct": correct, "total": total, "unsure_rows": unsure_flags,
            "extra_rows": extra, "errors": missed}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    labels = json.loads((SAMPLES / "labels.json").read_text())
    names = sys.argv[1:] or sorted(labels)
    all_correct = all_total = 0
    times = []
    for name in names:
        result = read_tally(str(SAMPLES / name))
        s = score_sheet(labels[name]["rows"], result["tally"]["rows"])
        all_correct += s["correct"]
        all_total += s["total"]
        times.append(result["seconds"])
        print(f"{name} [{labels[name]['difficulty']}]: {s['correct']}/{s['total']} fields, "
              f"{result['seconds']}s, unsure rows {s['unsure_rows']}, extra rows {s['extra_rows']}")
        for e in s["errors"]:
            print("   x", e)
    print(f"\nModel {MODEL}: {all_correct}/{all_total} fields correct "
          f"({all_correct / all_total:.0%}), avg {sum(times) / len(times):.1f}s per photo")

"""
Read a photo of a handwritten tally sheet into table rows, using Gemma
running locally through Ollama. Nothing leaves the laptop.

Use from Python:
    from extract.read_tally import read_tally
    result = read_tally("data/samples/tally_01.jpg")

Or from the terminal:
    uv run python -m extract.read_tally data/samples/tally_01.jpg
"""

import json
import sys
import time
from typing import Optional

import ollama
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

MODEL = "gemma4:e4b"     # change here to try a bigger/smaller Gemma

# The vendor's known items. In the app this comes from their sales history,
# so Gemma can map scribbles like "toms" or "sourdo" to a real item name.
KNOWN_ITEMS = ["kale", "tomatoes", "strawberries", "zucchini", "apples",
               "eggs", "sourdough", "honey"]


# The exact shape we want back. Ollama forces Gemma's answer to match it.
class Row(BaseModel):
    written_as: str = Field(description="item name exactly as written on the sheet")
    item: str = Field(description="matching name from the known item list, or 'unknown'")
    brought: Optional[int] = Field(description="quantity taken to market")
    sold: Optional[int] = Field(description="quantity sold")
    price: Optional[float] = Field(description="price per unit")
    unsure: bool = Field(description="true if any value in this row was hard to read")


class Tally(BaseModel):
    date_as_written: str
    market_as_written: str
    rows: list[Row]


PROMPT = f"""This is a photo of a market vendor's handwritten sales tally.
Read every item row into the schema.

Rules:
- Columns are: item, quantity brought (may be headed "took", "in" or "brought"),
  quantity sold, and price per unit (may be headed "$", "@" or "price").
- If a number is crossed out, ignore it and use the number written next to it.
- If "sold" says "all", "SOLD OUT" or similar, sold equals brought.
- Map each item to one of these known items: {", ".join(KNOWN_ITEMS)}.
  Abbreviations are common (e.g. "toms" = tomatoes). Use "unknown" if none fit.
- Set unsure=true for any row you could not read confidently. Never guess silently.
"""


def read_tally(image_path: str, model: str = MODEL) -> dict:
    """Send one photo to local Gemma and return its reading plus timing."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = ollama.chat(
        model=model,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT, "images": [image_path]}],
        format=Tally.model_json_schema(),
        options={"temperature": 0},
    )
    seconds = time.perf_counter() - start
    tally = Tally.model_validate_json(response.message.content)

    # "all" / "SOLD OUT" safety net, in case the model left sold empty.
    for row in tally.rows:
        if row.sold is None and row.brought is not None and not row.unsure:
            row.unsure = True
    return {"tally": tally.model_dump(), "seconds": round(seconds, 1), "model": model}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(read_tally(sys.argv[1]), indent=2))

content.text:
I've committed the project (one local commit, not pushed) and moved on to Gemma.

**Sample tallies:** I couldn't find any usable photos online. Nothing with a free license looked like a vendor's tally sheet, and scoring Gemma needs pictures where we know the right answers. So [make_tallies.py](data/samples/make_tallies.py) draws 12 tally photos from our simulated sales. They use free handwriting fonts and look like phone photos: tilted page, shadows, blur, crossed-out numbers and "all!" for sellouts. The correct answers are in `labels.json`. Everything is labelled as simulated, and real handwriting will be harder; I'll say that in the post.

**Gemma test:** `gemma4:e4b` is downloaded. [read_tally.py](extract/read_tally.py) sends a photo to Gemma on your laptop and gets table rows back, and [score.py](extract/score.py) checks them against the answers. The first run on two sheets got **48% of fields right**, at about 40 seconds per photo.
- Gemma reads the digits correctly but puts them on the wrong row.
- Because the photo is tilted, the numbers sit lower than their item names, so every value slips down one row.
- I've added an instruction telling it to follow the slanted lines, and that test is running in the background now. If the instruction doesn't fix it, the next step is to straighten the photo before sending it to Gemma.

The failure and the timings are logged in [EVIDENCE.md](EVIDENCE.md).

**Also:** sessions in this window aren't being recorded by Entire yet. Restart VS Code when you reach a good stopping point and that's fixed.

# so Gemma can map scribbles like "toms" or "sourdo" to a real item name.
KNOWN_ITEMS = ["kale", "tomatoes", "strawberries", "zucchini", "apples",
               "eggs", "sourdough", "honey"]


# The exact shape we want back. Ollama forces Gemma's answer to match it.
class Row(BaseModel):
    written_as: str = Field(description="item name exactly as written on the sheet")
    item: str = Field(description="matching name from the known item list, or 'unknown'")
    brought: Optional[int] = Field(description="quantity taken to market")
    sold: Optional[int] = Field(description="quantity sold")
    price: Optional[float] = Field(description="price per unit")
    unsure: bool = Field(description="true if any value in this row was hard to read")


class Tally(BaseModel):
    date_as_written: str
    market_as_written: str
    rows: list[Row]


PROMPT = f"""This is a photo of a market vendor's handwritten sales tally.
Read every item row into the schema.

Rules:
- The photo is usually tilted. Each row's values sit on the SAME ruled line
  as the item name, so follow that line across the page even if it slopes.
  Do not read straight across horizontally. The first row under the
  headers belongs to the first item.
- Columns are: item, quantity brought (may be headed "took", "in" or "brought"),
  quantity sold, and price per unit (may be headed "$", "@" or "price").
- If a number is crossed out, ignore it and use the number written next to it.
- If "sold" says "all", "SOLD OUT" or similar, sold equals brought.
- Map each item to one of these known items: {", ".join(KNOWN_ITEMS)}.
  Abbreviations are common (e.g. "toms" = tomatoes). Use "unknown" if none fit.
- Set unsure=true for any row you could not read confidently. Never guess silently.
"""


def read_tally(image_path: str, model: str = MODEL) -> dict:
    """Send one photo to local Gemma and return its reading plus timing."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = ollama.chat(
        model=model,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT, "images": [image_path]}],
        format=Tally.model_json_schema(),
        options={"temperature": 0},
    )
    seconds = time.perf_counter() - start
    tally = Tally.model_validate_json(response.message.content)

    # "all" / "SOLD OUT" safety net, in case the model left sold empty.
    for row in tally.rows:
        if row.sold is None and row.brought is not None and not row.unsure:
            row.unsure = True
    return {"tally": tally.model_dump(), "seconds": round(seconds, 1), "model": model}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(read_tally(sys.argv[1]), indent=2))

"""
Straighten a tilted tally photo so each row runs level across the page.

Why: Gemma reads rows straight across. On a tilted photo the numbers on the
right sit lower than their item name, so values slip into the next row.
Rotating the page level first fixes that.

How: try small rotations and keep the one where dark pixels (ink and ruled
lines) line up best into horizontal stripes, i.e. where the row-by-row
darkness varies the most. Plain numpy, no extra model.
"""

import io

import numpy as np
from PIL import Image, ImageOps


def find_tilt(img: Image.Image) -> float:
    small = ImageOps.grayscale(img)
    small.thumbnail((600, 600))
    dark = 255 - np.asarray(small, dtype=float)       # ink is bright here
    best_angle, best_score = 0.0, -1.0
    for angle in np.arange(-12, 12.01, 0.5):
        rotated = Image.fromarray(dark.astype("uint8")).rotate(angle, resample=Image.BILINEAR)
        rows = np.asarray(rotated, dtype=float).sum(axis=1)
        score = np.var(np.diff(rows))                  # sharp stripes = level page
        if score > best_score:
            best_angle, best_score = float(angle), score
    return best_angle


def straighten(image_path: str) -> tuple[bytes, float]:
    """Return the levelled image as JPEG bytes, plus the angle corrected."""
    img = ImageOps.exif_transpose(Image.open(image_path)).convert("RGB")
    angle = find_tilt(img)
    level = img.rotate(angle, resample=Image.BICUBIC, expand=True, fillcolor=(255, 255, 255))
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    level.save(buf, format="JPEG", quality=92)
    return buf.getvalue(), angle

"""
Turn a vendor's sales history into "how much to bring" per item, with TabPFN
running locally.

Key ideas, in plain words:
  * Features only use what the vendor knows BEFORE market day: past sales,
    which market, time of year, and the expected weather they type in.
  * TabPFN gives a range (quantiles), not one number.
  * The recommendation picks a point in that range per item: if an item has a
    big margin, running out costs more than a leftover, so we lean higher.
    (This is the classic "newsvendor" rule: quantile = margin / price.)
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from tabpfn import TabPFNRegressor
from tabpfn.constants import ModelVersion

from forecast.config import MODEL_VERSION

FEATURES = ["market_code", "item_code", "week_sin", "week_cos", "temp_max_c",
            "rain_mm", "holiday_week", "lag1_sold", "lag1_sold_out",
            "mean3_sold", "max3_sold", "days_since_start"]
QUANTILES = [round(q, 2) for q in np.arange(0.05, 0.96, 0.05)]


def add_features(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add model inputs. Lags are per (market, item) and only look backwards."""
    df = df.sort_values("date").copy()
    d = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    week = d.dt.isocalendar().week.astype(float)
    df["week_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * week / 52)
    df["week_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * week / 52)
    df["days_since_start"] = (d - d.min()).dt.days
    df["market_code"] = df["market"].astype("category").cat.codes
    df["item_code"] = df["item"].astype("category").cat.codes
    df["holiday_week"] = df["holiday_week"].astype(int)
    g = df.groupby(["market", "item"])
    df["lag1_sold"] = g["sold"].shift(1)
    df["lag1_sold_out"] = g["sold_out"].shift(1).astype(float)
    df["mean3_sold"] = g["sold"].transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean())
    df["max3_sold"] = g["sold"].transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(3, min_periods=1).max())
    return df


def make_model() -> TabPFNRegressor:
    version = {"v3.5": ModelVersion.V3_5, "v2": ModelVersion.V2}[MODEL_VERSION]
    return TabPFNRegressor.create_default_for_version(version)


def recommend(train: pd.DataFrame, upcoming: pd.DataFrame, model=None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Fit on past rows, predict the upcoming market's rows.

    Returns upcoming rows with low / typical / high and a `bring` quantity.
    """
    model = model or make_model()
    train = train.dropna(subset=["lag1_sold"])
    model.fit(train[FEATURES], train["sold"])
    q = np.array(model.predict(upcoming[FEATURES], output_type="quantiles", quantiles=QUANTILES))
    out = upcoming.copy()
    out["low"] = np.round(q[QUANTILES.index(0.1)])
    out["typical"] = np.round(q[QUANTILES.index(0.5)])
    out["high"] = np.round(q[QUANTILES.index(0.9)])
    # Newsvendor quantile per item: margin / price, kept within 0.5 to 0.9.
    target_q = ((out["price"] - out["unit_cost"]) / out["price"]).clip(0.5, 0.9)
    idx = [min(range(len(QUANTILES)), key=lambda i: abs(QUANTILES[i] - t)) for t in target_q]
    out["bring"] = np.ceil([q[i, row] for row, i in enumerate(idx)]).astype(int)
    return out

toolUseResult.content:
"""
Turn a vendor's sales history into "how much to bring" per item, with TabPFN
running locally.

Key ideas, in plain words:
  * Features only use what the vendor knows BEFORE market day: past sales,
    which market, time of year, and the expected weather they type in.
  * TabPFN gives a range (quantiles), not one number.
  * The recommendation picks a point in that range per item: if an item has a
    big margin, running out costs more than a leftover, so we lean higher.
    (This is the classic "newsvendor" rule: quantile = margin / price.)
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from tabpfn import TabPFNRegressor
from tabpfn.constants import ModelVersion

from forecast.config import MODEL_VERSION

FEATURES = ["market_code", "item_code", "week_sin", "week_cos", "temp_max_c",
            "rain_mm", "holiday_week", "lag1_sold", "lag1_sold_out",
            "mean3_sold", "max3_sold", "days_since_start"]
QUANTILES = [round(q, 2) for q in np.arange(0.05, 0.96, 0.05)]


def add_features(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add model inputs. Lags are per (market, item) and only look backwards."""
    df = df.sort_values("date").copy()
    d = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    week = d.dt.isocalendar().week.astype(float)
    df["week_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * week / 52)
    df["week_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * week / 52)
    df["days_since_start"] = (d - d.min()).dt.days
    df["market_code"] = df["market"].astype("category").cat.codes
    df["item_code"] = df["item"].astype("category").cat.codes
    df["holiday_week"] = df["holiday_week"].astype(int)
    g = df.groupby(["market", "item"])
    df["lag1_sold"] = g["sold"].shift(1)
    df["lag1_sold_out"] = g["sold_out"].shift(1).astype(float)
    df["mean3_sold"] = g["sold"].transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean())
    df["max3_sold"] = g["sold"].transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(3, min_periods=1).max())
    return df


def make_model() -> TabPFNRegressor:
    version = {"v3.5": ModelVersion.V3_5, "v2": ModelVersion.V2}[MODEL_VERSION]
    return TabPFNRegressor.create_default_for_version(version)


def recommend(train: pd.DataFrame, upcoming: pd.DataFrame, model=None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Fit on past rows, predict the upcoming market's rows.

    Returns upcoming rows with low / typical / high and a `bring` quantity.
    """
    model = model or make_model()
    train = train.dropna(subset=["lag1_sold"])
    model.fit(train[FEATURES], train["sold"])
    q = np.array(model.predict(upcoming[FEATURES], output_type="quantiles", quantiles=QUANTILES))
    out = upcoming.copy()
    out["low"] = np.round(q[QUANTILES.index(0.1)])
    out["typical"] = np.round(q[QUANTILES.index(0.5)])
    out["high"] = np.round(q[QUANTILES.index(0.9)])
    # Newsvendor quantile per item: margin / price, kept within 0.5 to 0.9.
    target_q = ((out["price"] - out["unit_cost"]) / out["price"]).clip(0.5, 0.9)
    idx = [min(range(len(QUANTILES)), key=lambda i: abs(QUANTILES[i] - t)) for t in target_q]
    out["bring"] = np.ceil([q[i, row] for row, i in enumerate(idx)]).astype(int)
    return out

toolUseResult.originalFile:
"""
Turn a vendor's sales history into "how much to bring" per item, with TabPFN
running locally.

Key ideas, in plain words:
  * Features only use what the vendor knows BEFORE market day: past sales,
    which market, time of year, and the expected weather they type in.
  * TabPFN gives a range (quantiles), not one number.
  * The recommendation picks a point in that range per item: if an item has a
    big margin, running out costs more than a leftover, so we lean higher.
    (This is the classic "newsvendor" rule: quantile = margin / price.)
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from tabpfn import TabPFNRegressor
from tabpfn.constants import ModelVersion

from forecast.config import MODEL_VERSION

FEATURES = ["market_code", "item_code", "week_sin", "week_cos", "temp_max_c",
            "rain_mm", "holiday_week", "lag1_sold", "lag1_sold_out",
            "mean3_sold", "max3_sold", "days_since_start"]
QUANTILES = [round(q, 2) for q in np.arange(0.05, 0.96, 0.05)]


def add_features(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add model inputs. Lags are per (market, item) and only look backwards."""
    df = df.sort_values("date").copy()
    d = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    week = d.dt.isocalendar().week.astype(float)
    df["week_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * week / 52)
    df["week_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * week / 52)
    df["days_since_start"] = (d - d.min()).dt.days
    df["market_code"] = df["market"].astype("category").cat.codes
    df["item_code"] = df["item"].astype("category").cat.codes
    df["holiday_week"] = df["holiday_week"].astype(int)
    g = df.groupby(["market", "item"])
    df["lag1_sold"] = g["sold"].shift(1)
    df["lag1_sold_out"] = g["sold_out"].shift(1).astype(float)
    df["mean3_sold"] = g["sold"].transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean())
    df["max3_sold"] = g["sold"].transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(3, min_periods=1).max())
    return df


def make_model() -> TabPFNRegressor:
    version = {"v3.5": ModelVersion.V3_5, "v2": ModelVersion.V2}[MODEL_VERSION]
    return TabPFNRegressor.create_default_for_version(version)


def recommend(train: pd.DataFrame, upcoming: pd.DataFrame, model=None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Fit on past rows, predict the upcoming market's rows.

    Returns upcoming rows with low / typical / high and a `bring` quantity.
    """
    model = model or make_model()
    train = train.dropna(subset=["lag1_sold"])
    model.fit(train[FEATURES], train["sold"])
    q = np.array(model.predict(upcoming[FEATURES], output_type="quantiles", quantiles=QUANTILES))
    out = upcoming.copy()
    out["low"] = np.round(q[QUANTILES.index(0.1)])
    out["typical"] = np.round(q[QUANTILES.index(0.5)])
    out["high"] = np.round(q[QUANTILES.index(0.9)])
    # Newsvendor quantile per item: margin / price, kept within 0.5 to 0.9.
    target_q = ((out["price"] - out["unit_cost"]) / out["price"]).clip(0.5, 0.9)
    idx = [min(range(len(QUANTILES)), key=lambda i: abs(QUANTILES[i] - t)) for t in target_q]
    out["bring"] = np.ceil([q[i, row] for row, i in enumerate(idx)]).astype(int)
    return out

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

def _get_license_name(hf_repo_id: str) -> str:
    """Fetch the license_name from the HuggingFace API for a Prior-Labs repo.

    Uses the user's cached HuggingFace token (``HF_TOKEN`` env var or
    ``huggingface-cli login``) so gated repos resolve correctly. Raises
    :class:`TabPFNLicenseError` if the user has no HF access to the repo,
    the request fails, or the model card has no ``license_name``.
    """
    from huggingface_hub import get_token  # noqa: PLC0415

    url = f"https://huggingface.co/api/models/Prior-Labs/{hf_repo_id}"
    headers = {}
    token = get_token()
    if token:
        headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {token}"
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers=headers)
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10) as resp:  # noqa: S310
            data = json.loads(resp.read())
    except Exception as exc:
        raise TabPFNHuggingFaceGatedRepoError(f"Prior-Labs/{hf_repo_id}") from exc
    license_name = data.get("cardData", {}).get("license_name")
    if not license_name:
        raise TabPFNError(
            f"HuggingFace model card for Prior-Labs/{hf_repo_id} is missing "
            f"cardData.license_name. This is a server-side misconfiguration of "
            f"the model card; please report it to support@priorlabs.ai."
        )
    return license_name


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# License acceptance check
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def check_license_accepted(token: str, api_url: str, version: str) -> bool | None:
    """Check whether the user has accepted the TabPFN license.

    Returns:
    -------
    True
        License has been accepted.
    False
        License has not been accepted (or token invalid).
    None
        Server is unreachable — cannot verify.
    """
    encoded_version = urllib.parse.quote(version)
    url = f"{api_url.rstrip('/')}/account/license/?version={encoded_version}"
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"})  # noqa: S310
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10) as resp:  # noqa: S310
            data = json.loads(resp.read())
            return data.get("accepted", False)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
        if exc.code in (401, 403):
            return False
        logger.warning("Unexpected HTTP %s from license check endpoint", exc.code)
        return None
    except Exception:
        logger.debug("License check endpoint unreachable", exc_info=True)
        return None


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Terminal helpers (headless-interactive flow)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    if hf_repo_id in _accepted_repos:
        return True

    gui_url = settings.tabpfn.auth_gui_url
    api_url = settings.tabpfn.auth_api_url

    license_version = _get_license_name(hf_repo_id)

    token = get_cached_token()
    if token is not None:
        status = verify_token(token, api_url)
        if status is True:
            # Token is valid — now check license acceptance.
            license_status = check_license_accepted(token, api_url, license_version)
            if license_status is True:
                save_token(token)
                _accepted_repos.add(hf_repo_id)
                return True
            if license_status is None:
                raise TabPFNLicenseError(
                    "Could not reach the license server to verify acceptance.\n\n"
                    "Please check your internet connection and try again."
                )
            # license_status is False — license not yet accepted.
            # Fall through to browser login so the GUI can show the acceptance form.
            logger.info(
                "Token valid but license not accepted; opening browser for acceptance.",
            )
        elif status is None:
            raise TabPFNLicenseError(
                "Could not reach the license server to verify your token.\n\n"

    """Check whether the user has accepted the TabPFN license.

    Returns:
    -------

    False

    None
        Server is unreachable — cannot verify.

"""
Stall Sense: the app. Everything runs on this laptop (Gemma via Ollama,
TabPFN locally). No internet needed after setup.

Run:  uv run streamlit run app/app.py
"""

import sys
from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

ROOT = Path(__file__).parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from extract.read_tally import KNOWN_ITEMS, read_tally  # noqa: E402
from forecast.config import MODEL_VERSION  # noqa: E402
from forecast.model import add_features, recommend  # noqa: E402

HISTORY = ROOT / "data" / "history.csv"          # the vendor's own data (gitignored)
STARTER = ROOT / "data" / "synthetic" / "SIMULATED_sales_portland_or.csv"
UPLOADS = ROOT / "data" / "real" / "uploads"
DOCS = ROOT / "docs"

st.set_page_config(page_title="Stall Sense", page_icon="🧺", layout="wide")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# History: a plain CSV on this laptop
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\[redacted]_data
def load_history() -> pd.DataFrame:
    if not HISTORY.exists():
        pd.read_csv(STARTER).to_csv(HISTORY, index=False)   # demo starts from simulated data
    return pd.read_csv(HISTORY)


def save_rows(new_rows: pd.DataFrame):
    hist = pd.read_csv(HISTORY)
    pd.concat([hist, new_rows], ignore_index=True).to_csv(HISTORY, index=False)
    load_history.clear()


history = load_history()
simulated = (history["data_source"] == "SIMULATED").any()

st.title("🧺 Stall Sense")
st.caption("Know how much to bring to market. Runs fully on your laptop: "
           f"Gemma reads your tally, TabPFN ({MODEL_VERSION}) forecasts. Your sales never leave this machine.")
if simulated:
    st.info("Demo mode: history includes SIMULATED sales (real weather, made-up vendor). "
            "Add your own tallies to replace it.", icon="ℹ️")

tab_read, tab_plan, tab_bt = st.tabs(["📷 Read a tally", "📋 Next market load list", "📈 How well does it work?"])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Tab 1: photo -> Gemma -> editable table -> history
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def flag_problems(rows: pd.DataFrame, hist: pd.DataFrame) -> list[str]:
    """Simple checks, because Gemma never admits when it is unsure."""
    flags = []
    for _, r in rows.iterrows():
        issues = []
        if r["item"] not in KNOWN_ITEMS:
            issues.append("unknown item")
        if pd.isna(r["brought"]) or pd.isna(r["sold"]) or pd.isna(r["price"]):
            issues.append("missing value")
        elif r["sold"] > r["brought"]:
            issues.append("sold more than brought?")
        past = hist[hist["item"] == r["item"]]
        if len(past) and pd.notna(r["price"]):
            usual = past["price"].median()
            if abs(r["price"] - usual) > 0.3 * usual:
                issues.append(f"price unusual (usually {usual:g})")
        if len(past) and pd.notna(r["brought"]) and r["brought"] > 2 * past["brought"].max():
            issues.append("much more than ever before")
        flags.append(", ".join(issues) or "ok")
    return flags


with tab_read:
    st.subheader("Snap your tally after market")
    left, right = st.columns([1, 1.4])
    with left:
        photo = st.file_uploader("Tally photo", type=["jpg", "jpeg", "png"])
        sample = st.selectbox("...or try a sample (simulated) tally",
                              [""] + sorted(p.name for p in (ROOT / "data" / "samples").glob("tally_*.jpg")))
        path = None
        if photo:
            UPLOADS.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            path = UPLOADS / photo.name
            path.write_bytes(photo.getvalue())
        elif sample:
            path = ROOT / "data" / "samples" / sample
        if path:
            st.image(str(path), use_container_width=True)

    with right:
        if path and st.button("Read it with Gemma", type="primary"):
            with st.spinner("Gemma is reading your handwriting (about 20 seconds)..."):
                result = read_tally(str(path))
            st.session_state["reading"] = result
        result = st.session_state.get("reading")
        if result:
            t = result["tally"]
            st.caption(f"Read in {result['seconds']}s by {result['model']} on this laptop. "
                       f"Written as: \"{t['date_as_written']}\", \"{t['market_as_written']}\"")
            rows = pd.DataFrame(t["rows"])[["written_as", "item", "brought", "sold", "price"]]
            rows["check"] = flag_problems(rows, history)
            c1, c2 = st.columns(2)
            market_day = c1.date_input("Market date", value=date.today())
            market = c2.selectbox("Market", sorted(history["market"].unique()))
            st.write("Check and fix anything Gemma got wrong:")
            edited = st.data_editor(rows, num_rows="dynamic", use_container_width=True,
                                    column_config={"item": st.column_config.SelectboxColumn(options=KNOWN_ITEMS),
                                                   "check": st.column_config.TextColumn(disabled=True)})
            c3, c4 = st.columns(2)
            temp = c3.number_input("Max temperature that day (°C)", value=18.0)
            rain = c4.number_input("Rain that day (mm)", value=0.0, min_value=0.0)
            if st.button("Save to my history"):
                units = history.groupby("item")["unit"].first()
                costs = history.groupby("item")["unit_cost"].median()
                new = edited.drop(columns=["written_as", "check"]).dropna(subset=["brought", "sold"])
                new = new.assign(
                    date=market_day.isoformat(), weekday=market_day.strftime("%a"), market=market,
                    unit=new["item"].map(units), unit_cost=new["item"].map(costs),
                    leftover=new["brought"] - new["sold"], sold_out=new["sold"] >= new["brought"],
                    temp_max_c=temp, rain_mm=rain, holiday_week=False, data_source="REAL")
                save_rows(new)
                st.success(f"Saved {len(new)} rows. They will be used in the next forecast.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Tab 2: next market -> TabPFN -> load list
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def reason(hist: pd.DataFrame, market: str, item: str, rainy: bool) -> str:
    past = hist[(hist["market"] == market) & (hist["item"] == item)]
    similar = past[(past["rain_mm"] > 5) == rainy].tail(3)
    if similar.empty:
        return ""
    kind = "rainy" if rainy else "dry"
    lo, hi = int(similar["sold"].min()), int(similar["sold"].max())
    sold_out = int(similar["sold_out"].sum())
    note = f"last {len(similar)} {kind} markets you sold {lo} to {hi}"
    if sold_out:
        note += f" (sold out {sold_out}x, so demand was likely higher)"
    return note


with tab_plan:
    st.subheader("What should I load for the next market?")
    markets = sorted(history["market"].unique())
    c1, c2, c3, c4 = st.columns(4)
    market = c1.selectbox("Market", markets, key="plan_market")
    last_day = pd.to_datetime(history["date"]).max().date()
    day = c2.date_input("Date", value=last_day + timedelta(days=7))
    temp = c3.number_input("Expected max temp (°C)", value=18.0, key="plan_temp")
    rain = c4.number_input("Expected rain (mm)", value=0.0, min_value=0.0, key="plan_rain")
    holiday = st.checkbox("Holiday coming up this week")

    # Items this vendor has been selling at this market recently (in season).
    recent = history[(history["market"] == market) &
                     (pd.to_datetime(history["date"]) >= pd.Timestamp(last_day) - pd.Timedelta(days=35))]
    items = sorted(recent["item"].unique())
    items = st.multiselect("Items to bring", sorted(history["item"].unique()), default=items)

    if items and st.button("Make my load list", type="primary"):
        info = history.groupby("item")[["unit", "price", "unit_cost"]].last()
        upcoming = pd.DataFrame([{
            "date": day.isoformat(), "weekday": day.strftime("%a"), "market": market, "item": i,
            "unit": info.loc[i, "unit"], "price": info.loc[i, "price"], "unit_cost": info.loc[i, "unit_cost"],
            "temp_max_c": temp, "rain_mm": rain, "holiday_week": holiday, "data_source": "FORECAST",
        } for i in items])
        both = add_features(pd.concat([history, upcoming], ignore_index=True))
        train = both[both["data_source"] != "FORECAST"]
        target = both[both["data_source"] == "FORECAST"]
        with st.spinner(f"TabPFN {MODEL_VERSION} is forecasting on this laptop..."):
            rec = recommend(train, target)
        rec["why"] = [reason(history, market, i, rain > 5) for i in rec["item"]]
        out = rec[["item", "bring", "unit", "low", "high", "why"]].rename(
            columns={"low": "slow day", "high": "busy day"})
        st.dataframe(out, hide_index=True, use_container_width=True)
        st.caption("'Bring' leans above the typical day for items with a big margin: "
                   "running out costs you more than a leftover.")
        text = "\n".join(f"{r.item}: bring {r.bring} {r.unit}" for r in out.itertuples())
        st.download_button("Download load list", f"Load list for {market}, {day}\n\n{text}\n",
                           file_name=f"load_list_{day}.txt")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Tab 3: backtest results
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
with tab_bt:
    st.subheader("Would it have saved money? (backtest on SIMULATED data)")
    st.write("For every past market we trained only on earlier weeks, recommended a load, "
             "and replayed what would have sold. Compared with common rules of thumb:")
    files = sorted(DOCS.glob("backtest_v*.csv"))
    files = [f for f in files if not f.stem.endswith("_rows")]
    if not files:
        st.warning("Run `uv run python -m forecast.backtest` first.")
    else:
        pick = st.selectbox("Run", [f.stem for f in files], index=len(files) - 1)
        table = pd.read_csv(DOCS / f"{pick}.csv", index_col=0)
        table.index = table.index.map({
            "stall_sense": "Stall Sense", "last_sold": "Bring what I sold last time",
            "last_brought": "Bring what I brought last time",
            "vendor_actual": "Vendor's own pen-and-paper guess"}.get)
        st.dataframe(table, use_container_width=True)
        st.bar_chart(table[["waste_$", "lost_profit_$"]])
